claim: Autophagy is specifically induced in vaccine-induced antigen-specific CD8+ T cells in healthy human volunteers.
source: Here, we show that autophagy is specifically induced in vaccine-induced antigen-specific CD8+ T cells in healthy human volunteers.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Reduced IFNγ secretion by RSV-induced T cells in older vaccinees correlates with low autophagy levels.
source: In addition, reduced IFNγ secretion by RSV-induced T cells in older vaccinees correlates with low autophagy levels.
evidence: This correlation is stated in the abstract and supported by data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Levels of the endogenous autophagy-inducing metabolite spermidine fall in human T cells with age.
source: We demonstrate that levels of the endogenous autophagy-inducing metabolite spermidine fall in human T cells with age.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by GC-MS measurements shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Spermidine supplementation in T cells from old donors recovers their autophagy level and function, similar to young donors' cells.
source: Spermidine supplementation in T cells from old donors recovers their autophagy level and function, similar to young donors' cells, in which spermidine biosynthesis has been inhibited.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 3b-f.

claim: Endogenous spermidine maintains autophagy via the translation factor eIF5A and transcription factor TFEB.
source: Finally, our data show that endogenous spermidine maintains autophagy via the translation factor eIF5A and transcription factor TFEB.
evidence: This mechanistic pathway is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: The successful vaccination of the elderly against pathogens is considered one of the big challenges in our society.
source: However, the successful vaccination of the elderly against pathogens is considered one of the big challenges in our society (Weinberger, 2018; Chen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Most vaccines are less immunogenic and effective in the older population.
source: While most vaccines are less immunogenic and effective in the older population (Weinberger, 2018), little is known about the molecular mechanisms that underpin immune senescence.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Autophagy is thought to be one of the few cellular processes that underlie many facets of cellular aging including immune senescence.
source: Autophagy is thought to be one of the few cellular processes that underlie many facets of cellular aging including immune senescence (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Autophagy limits mitochondrial dysfunction and accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) by delivering unwanted cytoplasmic material to the lysosomes for degradation.
source: By delivering unwanted cytoplasmic material to the lysosomes for degradation, autophagy limits mitochondrial dysfunction and accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Rubinsztein et al., 2011).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Autophagy degrades protein aggregates that accumulate with age.
source: Autophagy degrades protein aggregates that accumulate with age and its age-related decline could contribute to 'inflamm-aging' (Salminen et al., 2012), the age-related increase in inflammatory cytokines in the blood and tissue.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Loss of autophagy strongly promotes production of the inflammatory cytokines TNFα, IL-6, and IL1-β.
source: Loss of autophagy strongly promotes production of the inflammatory cytokines TNFα, IL-6, and IL1-β (Saitoh et al., 2008; Stranks et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Autophagy levels decline with age in human peripheral CD8+ T cells.
source: We previously found autophagy levels decline with age in human peripheral CD8+ T cells (Phadwal et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Deletion of key autophagy genes leads to a prematurely aged immune phenotype, with loss of function in mouse memory CD8+ T cells.
source: Deletion of key autophagy genes leads to a prematurely aged immune phenotype, with loss of function in mouse memory CD8+ T cells (Xu et al., 2014; Puleston et al., 2014), hematopoietic stem cells (Mortensen et al., 2011), and macrophages (Stranks et al., 2015) with a myeloid bias (Mortensen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Autophagy-deficient immune cells accumulate ROS and damaged mitochondria.
source: In addition, we find in autophagy-deficient immune cells the same cellular phenotype that cells display in older organisms; they accumulate ROS and damaged mitochondria (Stranks et al., 2015; Puleston et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: CD8+ T memory responses from aged mice can be improved with spermidine.
source: Importantly, we can improve CD8+ T memory responses from aged mice with spermidine (Puleston et al., 2014), an endogenous metabolite synthesized from arginine.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Spermidine extends life-span via increased autophagy in yeast and other model organisms.
source: It was shown in yeast and other model organisms that spermidine extends life-span via increased autophagy (Madeo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Spermidine donates a residue for the hypusination of the translation factor eIF5a, which is necessary for the translation of TFEB.
source: Recently, we uncovered a novel pathway in which spermidine donates a residue for the hypusination of the translation factor eIF5a, which is necessary for the translation of a three proline motif present in the master transcription factor of autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis, called TFEB (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Treatment with bafilomycin A1 increases LC3-II in Jurkat cells by both flow cytometry and western blot.
source: In Jurkat cells, a human lymphocyte line, we confirmed that treatment with bafilomycin A1 increases LC3-II by both flow cytometry and western blot (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a and b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a and b.

claim: Bafilomycin A treatment leads to accumulation of LC3-II in PBMCs stimulated in vitro.
source: Similar results were obtained in PBMCs stimulated in vitro (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and d.

claim: Autophagic flux varies little within one individual between blood draws.
source: Taken together, the data show: (a) autophagic flux varies little within one individual between blood draws
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is limited variation in autophagic flux between individuals.
source: (b) there is limited variation between individuals
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Bafilomycin A treatment leads to accumulation of LC3-II in all cell types tested.
source: (c) bafilomycin A treatment leads to accumulation of LC3-II in all cell types
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: TCR/BCR/TLR or IFNγ-R stimulation weakly induces autophagic flux which is consistently further increased in the presence of bafilomycin A.
source: (d) the respective stimulations via TCR/BCR/TLR or IFNγ-R weakly induce autophagic flux which is consistently further increased in the presence of bafilomycin A.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: HCV-specific CD8+ T cells show a significant increase in autophagic flux at the peak magnitude of the T cell response to vaccination.
source: When measured at the peak magnitude of the T cell response to vaccination (2–4 weeks post Ad, 1 week post MVA) HCV-specific CD8+ T cells show a significant increase in autophagic flux that is not observed in HCV non-specific CD8+ T cells (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: In antigen-specific T cells, autophagic flux is highest shortly after vaccination but had declined to levels equivalent to antigen-non-specific T cells by the end of the study.
source: In antigen-specific T cells, autophagic flux is highest shortly after vaccination but had declined to levels equivalent to antigen-non-specific T cells cells by the end of the study (week 36 or 52).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Antigen exposure induces autophagic flux in the antigen-reactive CD8+ T cell subset in humans in vivo.
source: Together, these data show that antigen exposure induces autophagic flux in the antigen-reactive CD8+ T cell subset in humans in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the HCV vaccination data presented in Figure 1c.

claim: The naturally derived population of RSV-specific IFNγ-producing CD8+ T cells in peripheral circulation in response to the infection declines with age.
source: As expected, the naturally derived population of RSV-specific IFNγ-producing CD8+ T cells in peripheral circulation in response to the infection declines with age (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Bulk T cells of >60 year vaccinees showed significantly lower basal autophagic flux compared to younger vaccinees.
source: No MHC class I pentamers were available for RSV to identify antigen-specific T cells; however, bulk T cells of the >60 year vaccinees showed significantly lower basal autophagic flux (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: There is a strong inverse correlation between autophagy levels and IFNγ responses in aged vaccinees.
source: We correlated autophagy levels in T cells with IFNγ ELISpot responses in individual vaccinees and found a strong inverse correlation in the aged group (Figure 1e) between autophagy and IFNγ responses, but not in the young group (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is supported by correlation data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: There is no correlation between autophagy levels and IFNγ responses in young vaccinees.
source: We correlated autophagy levels in T cells with IFNγ ELISpot responses in individual vaccinees and found a strong inverse correlation in the aged group (Figure 1e) between autophagy and IFNγ responses, but not in the young group (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is supported by correlation data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Reduced T cell autophagy in aged T cells may underpin reduced T cell responses to vaccination.
source: Taken together these data suggest that reduced T cell autophagy in aged T cells may underpin reduced T cell responses to vaccination.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the correlation data in Figures 1d-f.

claim: Both intracellular IFNγ expression and secretion was significantly decreased in Atg7-deficient T cells.
source: Both intracellular IFNγ expression and secretion was significantly decreased in Atg7-deficient T cells (Figure 2a and b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2a and b from mouse experiments.

claim: Intracellular perforin expression was reduced in Atg7-deficient T cells.
source: Similarly, intracellular perforin expression was reduced in Atg7-deficient T cells (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2c from mouse experiments.

claim: Hydroxychloroquine inhibits autophagosomal-lysosomal fusion.
source: Next, we sought to confirm our data in human T cells using pharmacological autophagic flux inhibitors, namely hydroxychloroquine (HcQ) that inhibits autophagosomal-lysosomal fusion (Mauthe et al., 2018)
evidence: This mechanism is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: SBI-0206965 is an AMPK1 and Ulk1 inhibitor.
source: and the AMPK1 and Ulk1 inhibitor SBI-0206965 (SbI) (Dite et al., 2018; Egan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Pharmacological autophagy inhibitors reduce IFNγ production in human CD8+ T cells.
source: Using these drugs, we could recapitulate the data observed in the genetic mouse model of autophagy deletion showing an inhibition of IFNγ (Figure 2d and e) and perforin production (Figure 2f) in CD8+ T cells.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2d-f.

claim: Pharmacological autophagy inhibitors reduce perforin production in human CD8+ T cells.
source: Using these drugs, we could recapitulate the data observed in the genetic mouse model of autophagy deletion showing an inhibition of IFNγ (Figure 2d and e) and perforin production (Figure 2f) in CD8+ T cells.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Activation of autophagy by Resveratrol in human CD8+ T cells increases the production of IFNγ and perforin.
source: Conversely, activation of autophagy by Resveratrol (Res) (Rubinsztein et al., 2011; Morselli et al., 2010) in human CD8+ T cell increased the production of IFNγ and perforin (Figure 2g–i).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2g-i.

claim: Autophagy is required for CD8+ T cell function by controlling IFNγ and perforin production.
source: In summary, these data suggest that autophagy is required for CD8+ T cell function by controlling IFNγ and perforin production.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 2.

claim: There is an inverse correlation between age and spermidine levels in PBMCs.
source: Thus, we determined spermidine, spermine and putrescine levels in PBMCs by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS), and found an inverse correlation between age and spermidine but not with spermine or putrescine (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by GC-MS data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: There is no correlation between age and spermine levels in PBMCs.
source: Thus, we determined spermidine, spermine and putrescine levels in PBMCs by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS), and found an inverse correlation between age and spermidine but not with spermine or putrescine (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by GC-MS data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: There is no correlation between age and putrescine levels in PBMCs.
source: Thus, we determined spermidine, spermine and putrescine levels in PBMCs by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS), and found an inverse correlation between age and spermidine but not with spermine or putrescine (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by GC-MS data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Spermidine supplementation improves autophagic flux in T cells from old donors.
source: Both autophagic flux and the secretion of IFNγ measured by ELISA was improved significantly in T cells from older vaccinees (Figure 3b and c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Spermidine supplementation improves IFNγ secretion in T cells from old donors.
source: Both autophagic flux and the secretion of IFNγ measured by ELISA was improved significantly in T cells from older vaccinees (Figure 3b and c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Increased IFNγ can be detected after spermidine treatment by intracellular staining for flow cytometry.
source: Similarly, increased IFNγ can be detected after spermidine treatment by intracellular staining for flow cytometry (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Spermidine supplementation increases the expression of perforin in T cells from old donors.
source: Interestingly, spermidine supplementation also increases the expression of perforin (Figure 3e) but not of Granzyme B (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Spermidine supplementation does not increase the expression of Granzyme B in T cells from old donors.
source: Interestingly, spermidine supplementation also increases the expression of perforin (Figure 3e) but not of Granzyme B (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: Autophagy inhibitors ablate the rejuvenating effects of spermidine supplementation in old donor cells.
source: Moreover, to investigate whether spermidine acts through autophagy to improve CD8+ T cell function, we added spermidine together with pharmacological autophagy inhibitors. Indeed, HcQ or Sbl ablates the rejuvenating effects of spermidine supplementation in old donor cells (Figure 3c–f).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3c-f.

claim: Spermine does not rescue CD8+ T cell function from old donors.
source: In contrast, spermine, another polyamine from the same pathway, which is not significantly reduced with age (Figure 3a) and does not serve as a direct substrate for eIF5A hypusination (Lee and Park, 2000), does not rescue CD8+ T cell function from old donors (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a-c.

claim: Spermine does not serve as a direct substrate for eIF5A hypusination.
source: In contrast, spermine, another polyamine from the same pathway, which is not significantly reduced with age (Figure 3a) and does not serve as a direct substrate for eIF5A hypusination (Lee and Park, 2000), does not rescue CD8+ T cell function from old donors (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Spermidine treatment reduces mitochondrial mass in CD8+ T cells from old donors.
source: We indeed show that mitochondrial mass was reduced after spermidine treatment as assessed by MitoTracker Green (MTG) and nonylacridine orange (NAO) staining, two fluorescent probes which have been commonly used to assess mitochondrial mass (Doherty and Perl, 2017; Figure 3—figure supplement 2a and b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2a and b.

claim: Spermidine treatment does not alter mitochondrial membrane potential in CD8+ T cells from old donors.
source: Damaged or dysfunctional mitochondria often show altered membrane potential and increased ROS) production (Puleston et al., 2014); however, we did not observe any changes in these parameters after spermidine treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 2c and d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2c.

claim: Spermidine treatment does not alter mitochondrial ROS production in CD8+ T cells from old donors.
source: Damaged or dysfunctional mitochondria often show altered membrane potential and increased ROS) production (Puleston et al., 2014); however, we did not observe any changes in these parameters after spermidine treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 2c and d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2d.

claim: DFMO almost completely blocks autophagy in CD8+ T cells activated over 7 days.
source: Addition of DFMO almost completely blocked autophagy in CD8+ T cells activated over 7 days;, however, when cells were supplemented with spermidine autophagic flux was recovered (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Spermidine supplementation recovers autophagic flux in DFMO-treated CD8+ T cells.
source: Addition of DFMO almost completely blocked autophagy in CD8+ T cells activated over 7 days;, however, when cells were supplemented with spermidine autophagic flux was recovered (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: DFMO partially blocks IFNγ expression in anti-CD3/CD28 activated CD8+ T cells, which can be rescued by spermidine.
source: DFMO also partially blocks IFNγ and perforin expression in anti-CD3/CD28 activated CD8+ T cells, which can be rescued by spermidine (Figure 4b and c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: DFMO partially blocks perforin expression in anti-CD3/CD28 activated CD8+ T cells, which can be rescued by spermidine.
source: DFMO also partially blocks IFNγ and perforin expression in anti-CD3/CD28 activated CD8+ T cells, which can be rescued by spermidine (Figure 4b and c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Granzyme B expression is not affected by DFMO or spermidine supplementation.
source: As before, granzyme B expression was not affected by DFMO or spermidine supplementation (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: T cells from young donors do not respond to spermidine supplementation.
source: T cells from young donors, with their high endogenous spermidine levels, do not respond to spermidine supplementation (Figure 4e–g).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4e-g.

claim: GC7 inhibits the hypusinated/activated form of eIF5A in Jurkat cells.
source: We first verified in the human lymphocyte line Jurkat that the inhibitor GC7 inhibits the hypusinated/activated form of eIF5A (Figure 5a)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: GC7 decreases LC3-II expression in a dose-dependent manner in Jurkat cells.
source: and also confirmed that it decreases LC3-II expression in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: GC7 reduces TFEB and hypusinated eIF5A in CD8+ T cells activated for 4 days.
source: GC7 reduces TFEB and hypusinated eIF5A in CD8+ T cells activated for 4 days (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: GC7 diminishes the autophagic flux in activated CD8+ T cells over a time course of 7 days.
source: It also diminishes the autophagic flux in activated CD8+ T cells over a time course of 7 days (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: DFMO reduces hypusinated eIF5A and TFEB levels in PBMCs, which is rescued with spermidine.
source: While anti-CD3/CD28 increases expression levels of TFEB and eIF5A, a reduction of hypusinated eIF5A and TFEB levels in PBMCs treated with DFMO was observed, which is rescued with spermidine (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Spermidine treatment of PBMCs from young donors does not induce the eIF5A-TFEB pathway.
source: As expected, spermidine treatment of PBMCs from young donors demonstrated to have high levels of spermidine does not induce this pathway (Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Spermidine improves both eIF5A hypusination and TFEB expression two-fold in activated PBMCs from old donors.
source: Again, we observed that activation induces levels of protein expression of both hypusinated eIF5A and TFEB, and spermidine further improves both eIF5A and TFEB two-fold (Figure 5f).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5f.

claim: Both intracellular IFNγ and perforin expression were significantly decreased in Tfeb KO CD8+ T cells upon stimulation.
source: Interestingly, both intracellular IFNγ and perforin expression were significantly decreased in Tfeb KO CD8+ T cells upon stimulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2b and c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2b and c.

claim: Tfeb KO CD8+ T cells failed to upregulate IFNγ and perforin in the presence of spermidine.
source: Moreover, Tfeb KO CD8+ T cells failed to upregulate IFNγ and perforin in the presence of spermidine (Figure 5—figure supplement 2b and c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2b and c.

claim: Loss of TFEB has no impact on granzyme B expression.
source: Analogous to previous observation, loss of TFEB had no impact on granzyme B expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2d.

claim: TFEB itself is essential for T cell function.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that TFEB itself is essential for T cell function and that spermidine was unable to improve T cell function when TFEB was knocked out.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Tfeb knockout data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Spermidine is unable to improve T cell function when TFEB is knocked out.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that TFEB itself is essential for T cell function and that spermidine was unable to improve T cell function when TFEB was knocked out.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Tfeb knockout data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Autophagy is induced in human CD8+ T cells after in vivo antigen encounter during vaccination.
source: Here, we show for the first time that autophagy is indeed highly active in human CD8+ T cells after the in vivo encounter of antigens in donors from two different experimental vaccination trials.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data from HCV and RSV vaccination trials.

claim: Autophagy peaks after 4 days of anti-CD3/CD28 stimulation in human T cells.
source: While it has been shown in human T cells that autophagy peaks after 4 days of anti-CD3/CD28 stimulation, later time points are more difficult to mimic accurately in vitro.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to published literature (Watanabe et al., 2014).

claim: Antigenic encounter in vivo induces autophagy after the effector phase in human CD8+ T cells.
source: Here, we show for the first time that antigenic encounter in vivo induces autophagy after the effector phase, arguing that autophagy may be important in human CD8+ T cells during the memory phase.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the HCV vaccination data.

claim: There is no bystander effect on CD8+ T cells that are not specific for HCV, suggesting autophagy induction is a cell-intrinsic effect through specific TCR stimulation.
source: Interestingly, we could not observe any bystander effect on CD8+ T cells that are not specific for HCV, suggesting that it is a cell-intrinsic effect through specific stimulation via their TCR.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the HCV vaccination data in Figure 1c.

claim: Spermidine increases the autophagy-dependent selective degradation of mitochondria (mitophagy).
source: Our data is in agreement with previous reports showing that spermidine increases the autophagy-dependent selective degradation of mitochondria (mitophagy) and thus contributes to mitochondrial health and functionality (Eisenberg et al., 2016; García-Prat et al., 2016; Fan et al., 2017; Qi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: TFEB promotes autophagy and improves mitophagy turnover in neuronal and hepatocytes.
source: The positive impact on cellular mitochondrial content is in line with two recent studies showing that TFEB promotes autophagy and improves mitophagy turnover in neuronal and hepatocytes (Tan et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The number of people over 60 years of age is expected to double by 2050, reaching 2.1 billion worldwide.
source: With increasing life expectancy, the number of people over 60 years of age is expected to double by 2050, reaching 2.1 billion worldwide.
evidence: This is a demographic projection stated in the Discussion.

claim: The severity of many infections is higher in the older population compared to younger adults.
source: The severity of many infections is higher in the older population compared to younger adults as particularly notable during the SARS2-CoV pandemic.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is general medical knowledge.

claim: Immune responses to vaccines are known to be particularly ineffective in the older population.
source: Immune responses to vaccines are known to be particularly ineffective in the older population and yet some vaccines such as for influenza and SARS2-Cov are primarily needed for the older adults.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is established medical knowledge.

claim: Rapamycin was the first drug shown to have a beneficial effect on T cell responses in mice and older humans by targeting mTOR.
source: Targeting mTOR with Rapamycin was the first drug both in mice and in human clinical trials shown to have a beneficial effect on T cell responses in mice and older humans (Araki et al., 2009; Mannick et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Low autophagy levels correlate with low responses to vaccination in older humans.
source: With this study we show for the first time that the autophagy-inducing drug spermidine has an immune boosting effect on the T cell compartment in humans in vitro and that low autophagy levels correlate with low responses to vaccination.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by data from the RSV vaccination trial.

claim: The translation of TFEB is one of the limiting factors for sufficient autophagy levels required to mount an immune response.
source: The translation of TFEB is one of the limiting factors for sufficient autophagy levels required to mount an immune response.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by the eIF5A-TFEB pathway data.

claim: TFEB needs to be dephosphorylated for its translocation into the nucleus, which mTOR inhibition facilitates.
source: In addition, to be active, TFEB needs to be dephosphorylated for its translocation into the nucleus, which mTOR inhibition facilitates (Martina et al., 2012; Roczniak-Ferguson et al., 2012; Settembre et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Spermidine and an mTOR inhibitor may have to be combined to optimally restore immune responses in the older adults.
source: Therefore, spermidine and an mTOR inhibitor may have to be combined to optimally restore immune responses in the older adults.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed in the Discussion based on the mechanisms of spermidine and mTOR inhibition.

claim: Spermidine levels decline in PBMCs in older humans.
source: We find that spermidine levels decline in PBMCs in the older humans.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by GC-MS data in Figure 3a.

claim: Spermidine levels in plasma were found to be low in the >65 age group and rising again in centenarians.
source: This confirms earlier study in plasma in which spermidine levels were found to be low in the >65 age group and rising again in centenarians (Pucciarelli et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Spermidine has been administered to humans in a small experimental trial with a beneficial effect on cognitive function without adverse effects.
source: Spermidine has recently been administered to humans in a small experimental trial with a beneficial effect on cognitive function without adverse effects (Schwarz et al., 2018; Wirth et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: eIF5A, TFEB and autophagy in PBMCs could be used as biomarkers for the antiaging effect of spermidine and related drugs during vaccination.
source: Furthermore, this trial could help to determine if eIF5A, TFEB and autophagy in PBMCs could be used as biomarkers for the antiaging effect of spermidine and related drugs during vaccination.
evidence: This is a proposal for future research stated in the Discussion.

claim: The vaccination protocol in older adults could in the future be adjusted according to whether the spermidine-eIF5A-TFEB pathway is functional in individual vaccinees.
source: Based on this information, the vaccination protocol in older adults could in the future be adjusted according to whether this pathway is functional in individual vaccinees.
evidence: This is a proposal for future clinical application stated in the Discussion.

claim: A novel anti-immune senescence pathway in humans with druggable targets and biomarkers has been validated.
source: In conclusion, we validated a novel anti-immune senescence pathway in humans with druggable targets and biomarkers, which could also be used for other broader anti-aging drug trials.
evidence: This is the concluding statement summarizing the findings of the study.

claim: Human TFEB contains two triproline motifs while mouse TFEB contains one.
source: One such triproline motif-containing protein is TFEB, with mouse TFEB containing one triproline motif while human TFEB contains two.
evidence: This is a structural comparison stated in the Results section.

claim: TFEB is the key master transcription factor of autophagosomal and lysosomal gene expression.
source: TFEB is the key master transcription factor of autophagosomal and lysosomal gene expression (Napolitano and Ballabio, 2016; Lapierre et al., 2015; Settembre et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: eIF5A promotes the translation of polyproline-rich domains in addition to its role in initiation and termination.
source: Spermidine provides a moiety to the translation factor eIF5A, which in addition to its role in initiation and termination also promotes the translation of polyproline-rich domains, which are difficult to translate (Gutierrez et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Deletion of autophagy mostly affects T cells in the memory phase of CD8+ T cell responses as opposed to the effector phase.
source: In line with this, we and Xu et al showed that deletion of autophagy mostly affects T cells in the memory phase of CD8+ T cell responses as opposed to the effector phase (Xu et al., 2014; Puleston et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature including the authors' previous work.

claim: The memory response in autophagy-deficient T cells could be rescued by N-acetyl cysteine.
source: Interestingly, the work of Schlie et al., 2015 showed that the memory response could be rescued by N-acetyl cysteine, arguing that memory cells may be formed but not maintained without autophagy.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.
